query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled rapid quench, by substantially increasing the cooling rate during solidification of eutectic high-entropy alloys, will refine the lamellar spacing and improve phase boundary coherence, thereby simultaneously enhancing both the strength and ductility compared to alloys processed at conventional cooling rates.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy with a lamellar fcc/B2 or fcc/BCC microstructure produced by standard cooling rates, in which the trade-off between strength and ductility is typically observed.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermal treatment featuring a significantly higher cooling rate (rapid quench) during solidification.
generation.conditions: Room temperature and under monotonic tensile loading conditions typical for structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellar spacing and more coherent (optimized) phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The rapid quench is expected to inhibit coarsening of the lamellar structure, leading to a finer dispersion of hard and soft phases. This refinement increases the strength via enhanced interface (or lamellar) strengthening while the improved phase boundary structure enables more uniform dislocation motion, which in turn enhances ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the rapid quench processed material is predicted to exhibit higher yield strength (due to interface strengthening) and greater ductility (due to improved dislocation mobility) simultaneously, surpassing the performance of conventionally cooled eutectic HEAs.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloy produced via standard cooling rates that yield a coarser lamellar microstructure with a trade-off between strength and ductility.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected when the cooling rate exceeds the conventional processing threshold but remains within the range that avoids inducing excessive residual stresses or other detrimental defects. The optimum cooling rate window is yet to be precisely defined.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold for the cooling rate that optimally balances the refinement of the lamellar structure without introducing adverse effects is not fully established. Moreover, the sensitivity of the resulting phase boundary coherence to rapid quenching conditions requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples with identical compositions. Process one set using a conventional cooling rate and the other set using a significantly increased cooling rate (rapid quench). Characterize the microstructures (using SEM/TEM) for lamellar spacing and phase boundary characteristics. Subsequently, perform room-temperature tensile tests on both sample sets to evaluate yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (fracture strain).
measurements: Lamellar spacing and phase boundary coherence (via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid quench processed samples do not show simultaneous improvements in both strength and ductility (i.e., if either yield strength or ductility is not significantly enhanced compared to the conventional samples) or if the microstructural analysis does not show a refined and coherent lamellar structure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Concurrent strength–ductility improvement of HfMoTaTiZr is achieved via Cr addition and the underlying strengthening mechanism was discussed. 4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase. The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 535.8 Hv 0.3 , 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr. The yield strength and fracture strain of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 reach 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa and 14.0 ± 2.9%, respectively, 207.5 MPa and 20.6% higher than HfMoTaTiZr. Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength and the formation of a reticulated structure of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 results in the improvement in ductility.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. chosen.technique: controlled rapid quench combined with selective low‐temperature annealing
chosen.conditions: Samples of eutectic high-entropy alloys processed in an inert atmosphere with a high cooling rate (>1000 K/s) and a brief annealing step to relieve residual stresses, followed by room-temperature tensile testing and microstructural characterization
chosen.why: Increasing the cooling rate directly refines the eutectic lamellar spacing and adjusts phase distributions, which is a well-established processing route. This intervention is experimentally tractable, fits within standard thermal treatment methods, and precisely addresses the open niche—simultaneously increasing strength (via grain refinement and dislocation blocking) and ductility (through a more homogeneous deformable microstructure) relative to a conventional cooling baseline.

frame.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase (lamellar) microstructures as typically produced for structural applications, where the current microstructure yields a compromise between strength and ductility.
frame.goal: Achieve a simultaneous increase in both strength and ductility relative to the conventional eutectic alloy baseline for structural applications.
frame.limitation: Standard processing routes yield a trade-off between strength and ductility, with enhancements to one property usually causing degradation of the other due to less-than-ideal phase boundary characteristics and lamellar spacing.

prior_attempts: Attempts involving multi-step processing or dual modifications (e.g., separately refining grain size and introducing precipitates) have improved one property at the expense of the other.

decision.trend: The earliest work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys (such as the AlCoCrFeNi system studied in PMC4145285) demonstrated that processing parameters (casting conditions, cooling rates, and moderate cold rolling) can tailor the lamellar microstructure to yield high strength and decent ductility. However, attempts that enhance strength by further refining the microstructure (through additional cold work) typically reduce ductility due to less‐ideal phase boundary characteristics. Over time, researchers have explored balancing these properties but the trade-off remains as a central challenge.
decision.unsolved: How to implement a single, unified intervention that simultaneously refines the lamellar spacing (for strength) while optimizing the phase boundary structure (for ductility) without resorting to multi-step or dual modifications remains unsolved.
decision.why: Following the trend, a controlled rapid quench (i.e., employing cooling rates significantly higher than conventional routes) is the most plausible next step. This approach is expected to finely refine lamellar spacing and induce more coherent phase boundaries, thereby enhancing both strength (via extensive interface strengthening) and ductility (by facilitating more uniform dislocation motion). This lever directly matches the niche analysis and responds to the open question under typical processing and structural service conditions.
